summary: The grouping is correct, the list alignment in deliver() holds, ByIdentity is sound, and no object-store request rate moves. What blocks is prose the commit falsifies and does not update: SegmentDelivery.segmentFanOut's javadoc still tells a reader the number publishSegment passes is a per-subscription OVER-COUNT that M5.40 will fix, which is now false and is the one paragraph a future FetchPolicy caller reads. Two further claims made by the commit itself are untrue: the fan-out change cannot flip any FetchMode at this call site, and the rejected linear scan is not quadratic at the stated scale.

findings.finding: The @param segmentFanOut javadoc still describes the PRE-CHANGE caller and this commit does not update it: 'a node subscribed to SEVERAL runs of the same segment appears once per subscription rather than once, so the count runs high for a multi-shard consumer. It biases toward `proxy` and `direct`, never toward `inline` ... M5.40 owns collapsing a node's subscriptions into one sink; until then this is an over-count, stated rather than hidden.' After this commit the only production caller passes exactly one entry per consumer, there is no over-count, and M5.40a is done. This is the contract doc of the very parameter whose meaning the commit changed, in the same module, and SubscriptionHub.java:376-383 now asserts the opposite of it eight lines from the call.
findings.failure_scenario: M5.43/M5.45b wires `direct`. Its author reads segmentFanOut's javadoc -- the only place the field's meaning is written down -- learns the value 'runs high for a multi-shard consumer' and 'biases toward proxy and direct', and compensates: raises directFanOutThreshold, or divides by an assumed runs-per-node, to absorb an inflation that no longer exists. The corrected threshold then elects DIRECT for fan-outs the policy should have served by PROXY, which is one consumer-side GET per node where one proxy read served all of them -- the exact spend M5.40/doc 10 s4 price, and invisible to the ingester's own CountingBinStore (GrantIssuer.java:140 records that it cannot be measured in this process). The repo has the precedent: M5.41's row records 'Two src/main javadocs that pointed a reader at M5.41 as the OPEN row are repointed in the same commit'.
findings.suggested_fix: Rewrite the 'WHAT M5.45a PASSES' paragraph to say what M5.40a made true -- one entry per consumer, no over-count -- and repoint the residual owner at M5.40b (per-node across separate publishes), which is the half still open.

findings.finding: The new comment claims a behaviour change that cannot occur at this call site: '`targets` used to hold one entry per (subscription, run), so a handful of nodes holding many runs each looked like a large fan-out and could tip `modeFor` into a different mode than the traffic warranted.' modeFor reads segmentFanOut only through wantsDirect (FetchPolicy.java:121-140), which requires servingPodUnderPressure OR !bytesInServingAz; this call site hardcodes `true` for bytesInServingAz and `false` for pressure, and the INLINE branch (FetchPolicy.java:84-89) depends only on batchBytes and bytesInServingAz. So no value of targets.size() has ever changed the mode here, before or after. The backlog cell restates it as '`SegmentDelivery`'s FAN-OUT MOVED WITH IT, which is a behaviour change beyond the bytes'.
findings.failure_scenario: A later session reading this comment believes the mode selection is fan-out sensitive on the held-bytes path and writes a regression test pinning a mode against a fan-out boundary. The test passes at every fan-out for the wrong reason -- the parameter is dead at this caller -- so it constrains nothing, and it will keep passing if the DIRECT arm (which throws IllegalStateException at SubscriptionHub.java:403) is ever made reachable by flipping bytesInServingAz. The direction is safe today: the number only ever got smaller and smaller cannot elect DIRECT here.
findings.suggested_fix: Say what is true: the number now counts byte streams, and it is not read by modeFor on this path because bytesInServingAz is always true here -- which is also why no test can see the change.

findings.finding: ByIdentity's javadoc rejects a linear scan as 'quadratic, and a segment carries on the order of 1,600 runs -- the same shape as a request rate that scales with runs, one layer in'. The scan is O(runs x consumers), and the row's own model puts consumers at ~9, so it is 1,600 x 9 reference comparisons -- linear in runs with a small constant. It is quadratic only when consumers scale with runs, which is the case the same row argues against. The trailing analogy is also backwards: the enclosing loop over committed.runs() already scales with runs, so scaling with runs is not by itself the forbidden shape here -- non-negotiable 6 governs object-store REQUESTS, and this loop issues none. (The construct itself is fine: java.util.IdentityHashMap is the JDK's identity-keyed map but does not preserve insertion order, which the LinkedHashMap comment at :369-371 needs, so ByIdentity + LinkedHashMap is justified -- the javadoc just never names the alternative a reader will reach for first.)
findings.failure_scenario: A future reader trusting 'quadratic' treats the grouping as a hot-path hazard and replaces it, or cites this paragraph as precedent that an in-memory O(runs) loop is 'the same shape' as a banned request rate -- which would rule out the run loop this very method depends on. Nothing breaks at runtime; the cost is a false rule propagated into the next design argument.
findings.suggested_fix: State the actual bound -- O(runs x consumers) against a map's O(runs) -- and drop the request-rate analogy, or name IdentityHashMap and why insertion order rules it out.

findings.finding: open's '@param pushes one per run of this segment that this subscriber holds, never empty' asserts a per-run uniqueness the code does not enforce. subscribe() does not deduplicate, so the SAME Subscriber instance registered twice against the same RunKey (two Subscription objects, two entries in the CopyOnWriteArrayList) is grouped into one ByIdentity bucket and the run is appended twice, so the list contains two identical Push records for one run.
findings.failure_scenario: M5.62's node-scoped subscriber re-subscribes a key without closing the old Subscription first (a takeover or a retry race). The node's single Subscriber then receives the same run twice in one open(); via assembling() the consumer callback is invoked twice with the same key, recordCount and firstOffset, and ConsumerClient.decodeInto enqueues that run's records twice from the same firstOffset -- duplicate records under offsets the commit log says appear once. Not a regression (the old contract delivered two pushes in two streams for the same shape), but the new javadoc now promises what the code does not, and M5.62 is the row that will rely on the promise.
findings.suggested_fix: Either dedupe the run list per consumer, or weaken the @param to 'one per SUBSCRIPTION this subscriber holds for a run of this segment'.

findings.finding: assembling()'s public javadoc is unchanged, but the adapter now aliases one byte[] across the K Push records it hands to onSegment (the sharing is documented only in an implementation comment inside complete(), not where a Consumer<Push> author reads). The 'O(SEGMENT) PER SUBSCRIBER' claim itself still holds and in fact got stronger -- one array per subscriber instead of one per subscription. What is new and unstated is that push.segment() is now shared, not private to that push.
findings.failure_scenario: A consumer callback that decodes or decompresses in place, or zeroes push.segment() after use (a reasonable reading of SegmentSink's 'a sink that needs to retain bytes copies them itself'), corrupts the other K-1 pushes it was handed in the same complete() call -- a silent decode failure or wrong records for every run but the first. No live defect today: the only decoder, ConsumerClient.decodeInto (client/src/main/java/binjava/client/ConsumerClient.java:76), opens the array read-only via SegmentReader.
findings.suggested_fix: One sentence on assembling()'s own javadoc: the array in every push of one segment is the SAME array, and a consumer that mutates it must copy first.

checked_and_clean: Grouping under concurrency: subscribers.get(run.key()) per run over a CopyOnWriteArrayList snapshot is the same window the per-run loop had -- a subscription closed mid-publish can still be served, and a subscription closed before its run is reached is not. Grouping across runs adds no window: Target holds the Subscriber rather than the Subscription, and neither the old nor the new code consulted liveness after gathering. The only new coupling is that declining one run now forfeits all K, which is the documented all-or-none contract.

ByIdentity is sound: an explicit equals/hashCode on a record suppresses the generated ones, so there is no conflict; identityHashCode is consistent with ==; and a hash collision between two distinct subscribers is resolved by the bucket's equals, so no LinkedHashMap entry can be lost. LinkedHashMap (not IdentityHashMap) is load-bearing -- AssembledServingPathFailureTest pairs sinks with subscriptions by index and would go order-nondeterministic under a hash order.

deliver()'s three lists cannot diverge: opened, pushes and live are appended in sequence only after open() returned non-null, both the null return and the catch continue before any append, and nothing between the three adds can throw. Index i is the same consumer in all three.

Cost: no object-store request rate moves. publishSegment still issues at most one read per segment per publish, independent of runs, shards, partitions and indices; the grouping is an in-memory map and adds no get/put/list/stat; the idle path still returns before any read via the targets.isEmpty() guard. The row's claim that the GET count was never the problem is correct and aSegmentOfMANYRunsIsReadONCENotOncePerRun covers it. Bytes pushed strictly decrease, from runs-per-segment to consumers-per-segment.

Arithmetic in the row and the new javadoc checks out: 1,600 x 8 MiB = 12,800 MiB = 12.5 GiB; 1,600 / 0.001 = 1.6e6, six orders; 178 x 8 MiB ~ 1.39 GiB; ~9 nodes at ~6x cross-AZ against 0.1% is 6,000x, three orders. The 'cannot reach 0.1%, so the criterion is proportionality' framing is right rather than a hedge.

The all-or-none failure semantics hold in code: Tracking marks a sink failed from the catch, deliver() skips completing it, and one sink per consumer means a mid-stream throw leaves a prefix that no run of that consumer is completed from.
